rows.answer: Mutual funds may avail intraday borrowing for all unitholder pay‑outs such as redemptions, IDCW pay‑outs, interest etc., for pay‑ins related to investments made by the scheme, for mark‑to‑market (MTM) obligations and foreign‑exchange settlements, and for repayment of existing borrowings [1][2].
The intraday borrowing conditions in the July 10, 2026 circular become effective on September 1, 2026.[3][1]
The cost of intraday borrowing, if any, is borne by the Asset Management Company (AMC) of the mutual fund. [1]

No, a mutual fund is prohibited from borrowing more than twenty percent of the net assets of a scheme; any borrowing must not exceed this 20% cap and must be for a maximum of six months, except for intraday borrowing which may be permitted under separate board‑specified conditions.[4] The Master Circular also requires that any borrowings above ten percent of net assets be disclosed, reinforcing the regulatory emphasis on limiting borrowing levels.[1]

The risk‑ometer for mutual fund schemes displays six risk levels: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High [2]. These levels correspond to risk‑value ranges where a value ≤ 1 is Low, > 1 to ≤ 2 is Low to Moderate, > 2 to ≤ 3 is Moderate, > 3 to ≤ 4 is Moderately High, > 4 to ≤ 5 is High and > 5 is Very High [3].
A Large Cap Fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in large‑cap stocks [6][5].

For an open‑ended scheme the Master Circular requires at least 20 investors and no single investor may hold more than 25 % of the scheme’s corpus[1]. These conditions are effective from 1 April 2026[1].
The certification examination for mutual fund distributors is conducted by the National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) [1].

The Master Circular for Mutual Funds identified as HO/24/13/11(1)2026‑IMD‑POD‑1/I/7602/2026, which was issued on 20 March 2026 and came into force on 1 April 2026, is the master circular presently in force, replacing the earlier circular dated June 27 2024.[1][7]
The Master Circular SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2020/156, issued on 24 August 2020 and effective from 24 August 2020, was the applicable master circular for mutual funds in January 2021.[1]

A Large Cap Fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in large‑cap stocks. [1][6]

The July 10 2026 circular superseded the earlier guidelines on borrowings of mutual funds that were set out in clause 5.9.1 of the SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated 20 March 2026 and also replaced SEBI Circular no. HO/(92)2026‑IMD‑POD‑2/I/7885/2026 dated 25 March 2026[1].

The Gazette Notification dated July 3 2026 (CG‑MH‑E‑07072026‑274229) amended the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 to permit intraday borrowings by mutual funds in order to address liquidity mismatches arising from differing market settlement timings. [2]
The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, and came into force on April 1 2026.[1][2]
The March 20, 2026 Master Circular replaces the Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated June 27, 2024.[1]
